extracted.intended_audience: school teachers, school directors/administrators, sanitary inspectors, and architects/building managers concerned with school ventilation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical sanitary and ventilation standards and recommendations for school-rooms to preserve health, prevent spread of infectious disease, and promote pupils' ability to study. Covers air sources of contamination, ventilator/window placement, humidity, dust control, maintenance, and administrative measures (inspection, exclusion of convalescents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent accumulation of epithelial scales (infective particles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epithelial cells or scales desquamated from skin, mouth, pharynx, and bronchi float in the air and are inhaled, carrying infectious agents (diphtheria, scarlatina, small-pox, measles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent their accumulation because greater numbers increase probability of successful transplantation of infection; remove them by adequate ventilation (air currents and ventilators) so they do not settle in favorable niduses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent accumulation of animal exhalations (odors) at ceiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutaneous and pulmonary 'animal exhalations' produce a heavy sickening smell that rises to the highest room portions and saturates air downward if not allowed to escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide outlets at high points (ceiling ventilators or high wall ventilators) to let these volatile noxious matters escape; example: removing tiles at roof apex immediately removed odor but showed pestilential atmosphere in attic—ventilate high spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient moisture (avoid overly dry air)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drier air increases evaporation from body liquids; a moderate dryness favors nervous temperament and development, but too dry an atmosphere is unhealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children themselves exhale much vapor (about half a pint each during school-hours) which helps add moisture in dry climates. Placing a shallow vessel of water on the stove may be of some service (water absorbs CO2 and large volumes of ammonia), though in many school-rooms it may be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize chalk-dust and inorganic dust suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Chalk-dust from blackboards floats in large quantities and, when inhaled, lodges in nasal passages and larynx causing irritation, tenacious mucus, cough, hawking and possible chronic catarrh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erase blackboards as little as possible; use 'dustless' (i.e., less dusty) erasers; erase gently in an up-and-down direction to avoid dispersing dust; sweep every evening and dust at least an hour before opening; avoid sweeping during the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweep and dust schedule to reduce airborne dust
rubrics_metrics.description: Dust and floor debris provoke coughs/sneezes when inhaled by audiences in enclosed spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sweep the school-room every evening and dust at least an hour before opening; do not disturb the floor by sweeping during the day to avoid releasing dust into occupied air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation fundamentals: temperature difference and diffusibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief factors carrying on ventilation are (a) difference in temperature between outside and inside air and (b) the diffusibility of gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use buoyancy of warmer indoor air to create upward currents and replace with cooler outside air; but when outside air is warmer the direction reverses, so design should account for seasonal variations and rely on both draughts and diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chimney/stove-pipe design for effective draught
rubrics_metrics.description: Draught up a flue is produced by higher temperature (lighter gases) of combustion products; pipe/flue geometry affects draught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pipes or flues should be vertical or nearly so and not too wide (wide pipes cause downward currents). Minimize elbows; use rounded rather than acute bends; two or more pipes opening into same chimney should ideally have separate flues to avoid interference and downward currents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place ventilators at highest points for exit of foul air
rubrics_metrics.description: Warmer, fouled air within has tendency to escape at highest points; ventilators should allow its exit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install ventilators at highest points of ceilings or walls near ceilings so foul gases can escape without creating drafts on pupils' shoulders; when a door is opened foul air escapes at top and fresh enters below—use this principle in design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide fresh-air inlets low in walls and outlets high
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresh cold air enters strongest at lowest openings while fouled warm air escapes at highest points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best method: ventilators in walls about a foot square, raised a few inches above the floor (inlet) and lowered a few inches below the ceiling (outlet), or ventilators in the ceiling. This arrangement avoids currents that blow on children's shoulders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window design and operation to avoid uncomfortable drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowering windows too low produces strong, uncomfortable draughts on pupils; windows set low in wall increase injurious draughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set windows high in the wall and lower them on the sheltered side when possible; use long, high windows arranged to slide upward from beneath and downward from above to control air movement and minimize direct draughts on pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muslin roller contrivance to prevent draughts through open windows
rubrics_metrics.description: A strip of unstarched muslin attached to a spring roller can be unrolled to stretch across the space when the window is lowered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holds tense to shut off draughts while allowing escape of foul gases within and the slow, steady entrance of fresh air—practical device to prevent direct shoulder-cooling draughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid placing ventilators in the hall
rubrics_metrics.description: Ventilators in the hall do little good because doors between hall and room often closed and buoyancy effects are nearly eliminated by partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put ventilators in the room's ceiling or walls near the ceiling rather than in the hall; otherwise animal exhalations will fill the room from ceiling down to level of top of communicating door and remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure adequate provision for fresh-air entrance separate from outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Outflow of inside air will not be rapid if there is not sufficient provision for entrance of fresh air other than through the same apertures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inlet and outlet apertures separately so diffusion alone isn't relied upon; provide both escape paths for foul air and dedicated inlets for fresh air to hasten interchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for seasonal reversal of air currents
rubrics_metrics.description: When outside air is warmer (e.g., hot summer day), the direction of currents may be reversed (fresh air coming in above and cool inside air escaping below).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that buoyancy changes with seasons; design ventilators and window operation to accommodate reversed flow conditions to maintain effective ventilation year-round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide high ceilings
rubrics_metrics.description: A school-room should have a high ceiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High ceilings help keep fouled warm air away from occupants and allow placement of ventilators high above pupils' heads; recommended in conjunction with adequate ventilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide 200–300 cubic feet of air per pupil
rubrics_metrics.description: A school-room should contain from two hundred to three hundred cubic feet of air to each pupil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design classroom volume and occupancy so each pupil has at least 200–300 cu ft of air to lessen fouling and reduce contagion risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send children outdoors at recess to renew air and clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: All children should be sent out at recess, even briefly, to expose clothing saturated by animal exhalations to open air and to allow doors and windows to be opened and air within changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recess as an opportunity to ventilate rooms thoroughly and reduce accumulated exhalations on clothing and in air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and prompt repair/reporting of heating/ventilation equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoves, chimneys, pipes, etc., should be carefully looked after and any accident or defect promptly attended to or immediately reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular inspection and maintenance prevent failures that could compromise ventilation or produce dangerous gases; include checks as part of school routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude convalescent children from school per contagiousness limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Children convalescing from contagious diseases should be excluded from school for weeks or months according to the recognized limit of contagiousness of the disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow recognized contagiousness limits to avoid introducing sources of infection into the school environment; administrative enforcement required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary inspection and remedial action for defective schools
rubrics_metrics.description: A sanitary inspection should be made of every school by a competent medical inspector; schools found defective in ways injurious to health should have defects remedied or be condemned for school purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement inspections, require remediation or condemn and impose penalties for continued use; remedies include ventilation improvements, rejection of unfit buildings, and enforcement by school directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize schools and churches as centers for contagious diseases and improve ventilation accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: School and church are two great centers for communication of contagious diseases and their activity in this way is directly proportional to the insufficiency of ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ventilation improvements in such public assembly spaces as a public-health priority to reduce disease spread; invest in ventilators and building modifications as effective preventive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit blackboard erasing and use less-dusty erasers
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackboards should be erased as little as possible and preferably by the so-called 'dustless' erasers—though no eraser is truly dustless, only less dusty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize blackboard dust production; when erasing, do so gently and in controlled directions (up-and-down) to avoid dispersal throughout room; consider alternative teaching materials or cleaning schedules to reduce airborne chalk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disturbing floor dust during occupancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The floor should not be disturbed by sweeping at any time during the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule sweeping for after hours to prevent resuspending dust into occupied air; perform dusting well before opening.
